content_html:
Social Security retirement benefits depend on two things you control: how much you earn over your career and the age at which you start collecting. This calculator applies the Social Security benefit formula to a simplified earnings history and shows your estimated monthly benefit at any claiming age from 62 to 70, in today's dollars. It is an estimate for planning only. Your official figure comes from the Social Security Administration (SSA), which uses your actual year-by-year earnings record.

How to use this calculator

  1. Birth year: sets your full retirement age.
  2. Average yearly earnings: your typical pay across your working life, in today's dollars.
  3. Years of work: how many years you will have paid Social Security tax by the time you claim. Only your 35 highest years count, and missing years count as zero.
  4. Claiming age: the age, in years and months, when you plan to start benefits.
  5. Life expectancy: used only to add up lifetime benefits so you can compare claiming ages.

How the estimate works

First, your earnings (capped at the $184,500 taxable maximum for 2026) are averaged over 35 years and turned into a monthly figure called average indexed monthly earnings (AIME). Next, the benefit formula replaces 90% of the first $1,286 of AIME, 32% of the amount between $1,286 and $7,749, and 15% of anything above. The result is your primary insurance amount: the benefit you would get at full retirement age. Because this shortcut treats today's wage cap as if it applied in every past year, it can overshoot for very high earners, so the estimate never goes above $4,152, the largest monthly benefit SSA pays at full retirement age in 2026.

Claiming early permanently lowers the benefit by 5/9 of 1% for each of the first 36 months before full retirement age and 5/12 of 1% for each month beyond that. Waiting past full retirement age adds 2/3 of 1% a month (8% a year) until age 70.

Worked example

Someone born in 1970 who earns an average of $60,000 a year for 35 years has an AIME of $5,000. The formula gives 90% of $1,286 plus 32% of $3,714, or $2,345.80 a month at full retirement age 67. Claiming at 62 cuts that to 70%, about $1,642 a month. Waiting until 70 raises it to 124%, about $2,908. If this person lives to 85, the lifetime totals are roughly $453,192 when claiming at 62, $506,520 at 67 and $523,440 at 70, before cost-of-living increases.

Tips for choosing a claiming age

  • Compare the lifetime totals in the table at a few different life expectancies. Delaying tends to pay off for people who live into their mid-80s or longer.
  • If you are married, the higher earner's claiming age also affects the survivor benefit the other spouse could receive.
  • Working fewer than 35 years leaves zeros in the average, so a few extra years of work can raise your benefit noticeably.
  • Check your real earnings record at ssa.gov and fix any missing years before relying on any estimate.

What this estimate leaves out

It assumes level earnings in today's dollars and ignores spousal and survivor benefits, the earnings test for people who work while claiming before full retirement age, income tax on benefits, and future cost-of-living adjustments. Benefits are also rounded down the way SSA rounds them, so small differences from other tools are normal.

faq.question: Is this the same number SSA will pay me?
faq.answer: No. This is a simplified estimate based on an average earnings figure and the 2026 benefit formula. SSA calculates your benefit from your actual year-by-year earnings record, indexed to wage growth, and the formula figures change every year. Sign in to your my Social Security account at ssa.gov for your official estimate.

faq.question: How many years do I need to work to qualify?
faq.answer: You generally need 40 credits to receive a retirement benefit. You can earn up to four credits a year, so most people qualify after about 10 years of work covered by Social Security.

faq.question: Why are benefits shown in today's dollars?
faq.answer: Using today's dollars keeps the figures comparable with your current income and expenses. Real benefits rise each year with cost-of-living adjustments, so the dollar amounts you receive later should be higher than shown, while their buying power should be similar.

faq.question: Can I change my mind after I start benefits?
faq.answer: Within 12 months of first claiming, you can withdraw your application once by repaying the benefits you received. After you reach full retirement age, you can also suspend benefits to earn delayed retirement credits until age 70.

faq.question: Does working while collecting reduce my benefit?
faq.answer: If you claim before full retirement age and keep working, SSA temporarily withholds part of your benefit once your earnings pass a yearly limit. Your benefit is recalculated upward at full retirement age to account for the withheld months. This calculator does not model that earnings test.
